items.prompt:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.
1. Disrupt that flushing, and the residue that should have been swept out — including the protein fragments associated with Alzheimer's — instead accumulates between neurons.
2. For decades, sleep was treated as little more than a passive idling of the brain, useful for rest but otherwise uninteresting to those studying cognition.
3. This re-framing has quietly turned the most basic of biological habits into one of the most consequential interventions we know.
4. That assumption began to crack in the 1990s, when researchers showed that the brain's clearance of metabolic waste depends on a flushing system that runs almost exclusively when we are asleep.
items.solution: Opener = A (states the old view of sleep; nothing precedes it). B follows A ("That assumption" → the old view). C follows B ("that flushing" → the system in B; consequence). Closer = D ("This re-framing" — broadening reflection). Sequence A-B-C-D = 2-4-1-3 = 2413.

items.prompt:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4) given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.

2. But this argument quietly assumes a strange picture of the self — one in which "I" am a passenger watching neurons fire, rather than the firing itself.
3. The standard objection to free will is now almost a cliché: if every thought is the product of prior brain states, then "I chose" is an illusion the brain narrates after the fact.
4. Drop that picture, and the supposed conflict softens; the choices my brain makes ARE the choices I make, because there is no second "me" standing apart to be deceived.
items.solution: Opener = A (states the standard objection to free will; nothing precedes it). B follows A ("this argument" → the objection). C follows B ("that picture" → the strange picture of self in B). Closer = D ("And so" — final reflection broadening from the argument). Sequence A-B-C-D = 3-2-4-1 = 3241. Opener trap: D sounds thesis-like, but "And so" forces it to close.

Flow, the absorbed state in which time seems to dissolve and effort feels effortless, is often pitched as the reward for matching one's skill to a sufficiently demanding task. Yet the celebration overlooks what flow leaves out. Inside it, the self that compares, doubts, and revises is quieted — useful for the immediate task, but the very faculty by which we judge whether a task is worth doing at all. Athletes and gamblers report flow alike; the experience tells us nothing about the value of what we are absorbed in. To pursue flow as an end is to risk perfecting our engagement with activities we have stopped examining.
options: Chasing flow suppresses the reflective faculty that asks whether an activity is worth doing — risking deeper engagement with pursuits we have stopped examining.
Flow is the rewarding state achieved when skill matches the demand of a sufficiently challenging task, dissolving the sense of time and effort.
Athletes and gamblers both report flow, which proves that the experience cannot be used as a guide to the moral worth of an activity.
Because flow quiets the self that doubts and revises, it must be avoided by anyone seriously committed to ethical reflection on how they spend their lives.
explanations: Correct. Essence: flow quiets the very faculty that judges whether an activity is worth doing, so chasing flow risks deepening engagement with unexamined pursuits. Economists insist that past expenditures should not influence present decisions: only future costs and benefits matter. People nonetheless persist in failing projects because they have already invested heavily in them, a habit dismissed as the sunk-cost fallacy. The label, however, may flatter the economists more than it explains the behaviour. Honouring past commitments sustains the credibility on which future cooperation depends; quitting too readily teaches partners that one's promises decay with circumstance. What looks irrational at the level of a single decision can be rational at the level of a reputation.

The sunk-cost fallacy is a label economists invented to flatter themselves, with no real bearing on how people actually behave under conditions of uncertainty.
